/-!
# Erdős Problem 225

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/225](https://www.erdosproblems.com/225)
- [Er40b] Erdős, P., *Note on some elementary properties of polynomials*. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc.
  (1940), 954-958.
- [Er57] Erdős, Paul, *Some unsolved problems*. Michigan Math. J. (1957), 291-300.
- [Er61] Erdős, Paul, *Some unsolved problems*. Magyar Tud. Akad. Mat. Kutató Int. Közl. (1961),
  221-254.
- [Ha74] Hayman, W. K., *Research problems in function theory: new problems*. (1974), 155-180.
- [Kr74] Kristiansen, G. K., *Proof of an inequality for trigonometric polynomials*. Proc. Amer.
  Math. Soc. (1974), 49-57.
- [SaSh74] Saff, E. B. and Sheil-Small, T., *Coefficient and integral mean estimates for
  algebraic and trigonometric polynomials with restricted zeros*. J. London Math. Soc. (2)
  (1974/75), 16-22.
- [Kr76] Kristiansen, G. K., *Erratum to "Proof of a polynomial conjecture"*. Proc. Amer. Math.
  Soc. (1976), 377.
-/

@[expose] public section

open Set

namespace Erdos225

/-- The trigonometric polynomial $f(z) = \sum_{0\leq k\leq n}c_k e^{ikz}$, as an entire function
of $z\in\mathbb{C}$. -/
noncomputable def trigPoly (n : ℕ) (c : ℕ → ℂ) (z : ℂ) : ℂ :=
  ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (n + 1), c k * Complex.exp (Complex.I * (k * z))

/--
Let
$$ f(\theta) = \sum_{0\leq k\leq n}c_k e^{ik\theta}$$
be a trigonometric polynomial all of whose roots are real, such that
$\max_{\theta\in [0,2\pi]}\lvert f(\theta)\rvert=1$. Then
$$\int_0^{2\pi}\lvert f(\theta)\rvert \mathrm{d}\theta \leq 4.$$

This is Problem 4.20 in [Ha74], where it is attributed to Erdős.

This was solved independently by Kristiansen [Kr74] (only in the case when $c_k\in\mathbb{R}$)
and Saff and Sheil-Small [SaSh74] (for general $c_k\in \mathbb{C}$). (The original proof of
Kristiansen contained an error which was later fixed in [Kr76].)

"All roots real" refers to the zeros of $f$ as an entire function of $\theta\in\mathbb{C}$. We
normalise by $c_0c_n\neq 0$ and $n\geq 1$: a factor $e^{im\theta}$ affects neither the zeros nor
$\lvert f\rvert$ on the real line, while a single term $c_me^{im\theta}$ has no zeros and
$\int_0^{2\pi}\lvert f\rvert = 2\pi$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 30 42, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos225.lean#L2034"]
theorem erdos_225 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (c : ℕ → ℂ), 0 < n → c 0 ≠ 0 → c n ≠ 0 →
    (∀ z : ℂ, trigPoly n c z = 0 → z.im = 0) →
    (∀ θ ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) (2 * Real.pi), ‖trigPoly n c θ‖ ≤ 1) →
    (∃ θ ∈ Icc (0 : ℝ) (2 * Real.pi), ‖trigPoly n c θ‖ = 1) →
    ∫ θ in (0 : ℝ)..(2 * Real.pi), ‖trigPoly n c θ‖ ≤ 4 := by
  sorry

end Erdos225

reformulations.difference: Lean uses a one-sided exponential sum with positive degree and nonzero endpoint coefficients. The primary literature uses classical trigonometric polynomials, interpreting the real-root condition as having all 2d zeros real in a fundamental period.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Writing P(w)=Σ c_k w^k gives trigPoly n c z=P(exp(iz)). With c_0≠0, all angular zeros are real exactly when all roots of P lie on the unit circle, since exp maps ℂ onto ℂ\{0} and |exp(iz)|=exp(-Im z). This is the class in Saff–Sheil-Small Theorem 1, whose q=1, M=1 specialization gives the asserted bound. Equivalence with their classical trigonometric formulation is also explicit: from a normalized one-sided sum f of degree n, form T(θ)=exp(-inθ)f(2θ), a trigonometric polynomial of degree n with 2n real zeros per period. It has the same maximum modulus and integral, by periodicity and substitution. Conversely, multiplying a classical degree-d trigonometric polynomial by exp(idθ) produces a one-sided sum of degree 2d. Trimming zero endpoint coefficients only factors out a zero-free exponential of real-line modulus one. The zero-free single-term cases excluded by Lean are not in the intended nondegenerate class.

review.notes: Both declarations were checked. Scratch Lean proofs verified the angular-root/unit-circle-root equivalence, the maximum formulation, continuity and interval integrability, small-degree expansions, and an admissible degree-one example. The full representation equivalence described above was checked mathematically, not completely formalized. The linked proof and its two local dependencies compiled in /workspace/review/verify-linked.lean; the cited theorem depends only on propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. The affirmative answer and solved status agree with the source. The exact [Ha74] chapter was not obtained, and publisher access blocked the [Kr74]/[Kr76] full texts; these access limitations do not prevent verification of either declaration against the available original Erdős papers and Saff–Sheil-Small.
